mercy_translation.text:
Therefore, when those who speak theologically about him say that he ate and drank and was born, understand that the body, as a body, was born and was nourished with appropriate food, while God the Word himself, who was united with the body, continued to order all things. Through the works he performed in the body he made himself known not as a mere human being but as God the Word. These things are said of him because the body that ate, was born, and suffered belonged not to someone else but to the Lord; and because, once he had become human, it was fitting that these things should be spoken of him as of a human being, so that he might be shown truly, and not merely in appearance, to possess a body.

But just as his bodily presence was known from these things, so from the works he performed through the body he made himself known as the Son of God. Therefore he cried out to the unbelieving Jews: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not believe me, believe my works, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

For just as, being invisible, he is known from the works of creation, so after becoming human and being seen in a body, he could be known from his works as the one who performed them—not a mere human being, but the Power and Word of God.

For when he commands demons and they are driven out, the work is not human but divine. And who, seeing him heal the diseases to which the human race is subject, would still consider him merely human and not God? He cleansed lepers, made the lame walk, opened the ears of the deaf, gave sight to the blind, and simply drove every disease and every weakness away from human beings. From these things anyone could behold his divinity.

Who, seeing him restore what was lacking to those whom nature had deprived from birth, and opening the eyes of the man blind from birth, would not understand that human birth itself lies subject to him, and that he is its Maker and Creator? For the one who restores what a human being did not possess from birth is plainly Lord also of human birth.

For this reason, when he first came down to us, he fashioned for himself the body from a virgin, so that he might give everyone no small sign of his divinity: the One who fashioned this body is also the Maker of the others. For who, seeing a body come from a virgin alone without a man, would not reason that the One appearing in that body is also the Maker and Lord of other bodies?

And who, seeing the substance of water changed and passing into wine, would not understand that the One who did this is Lord and Creator of the substance of all waters? For this reason, as Master he also stepped upon the sea and walked on it as on land, giving those who saw him a sign of his lordship over all things.

And when from a few things he fed so great a multitude, bringing abundance out of scarcity so that five thousand were satisfied from five loaves and as much again was left over, he made known nothing other than that he himself is the Lord of the providence of the universe.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius insists on the reality of Christ's body while simultaneously reading the miracles as signs of the Word's divine identity.
The biblical quotations are translated from Athanasius' wording rather than copied from a modern English Bible.
